title: write_errors_file truncates a red run's seal before it rewrites it, so every seal reader reads green in that window
body:
A red run's seal reads green for a moment before it reads red. `write_errors_file` (lib/runlog) writes a red run's seal in place: the extraction pipeline's `>"$errors"` truncates the seal when the pipeline starts, before anything is written into it (lib/runlog:716-717), and the tail fallback truncates it again when the extraction left it empty (lib/runlog:722-723). Until those writes land, the seal is an empty file. `seal_state`, the one classifier of a seal, reads an empty seal as green (lib/runlog:175-176). So any reader that lands in that window reads a red run as green, a false green, which is worse than a failure.

Every reader the window reaches:

- `seal_verdict` (lib/runlog:565), through `seal_state`, and through it `release_gates_verdict` (lib/release.steps:583). That is `release status`'s legs row, `release gates`' read of whether a sealed green already stands (it prints already and runs nothing), and a cut's start read and dry-run read of the local gates.
- lib/release.legs's three readers of a remote leg's GATES pair (lib/release.legs:441, 508, 526): a pair read while the remote run closes reads that leg green.
- `seal_disagreements` (lib/runlog:1714), through `seal_disagreement_reason`, over another gate's seal.
- `bin/.devbin/cmd/test`'s `--failed` (`run_failed`), which reads an empty newest bats seal as "no test failed in the last bats run" and runs nothing.
- Any person or agent reading a `LATEST_*.errors` seal by the house rule that empty is green.

A cut's own local leg no longer reads the seal while its run is alive. Since ST0011 WP02b-1 it decides on the run's exit status, so this window cannot tag a red release. It was found there, in that unit's critic-shell review (C0), and the review named the remedy below as outside the unit.

The remedy: write the red seal to a temp file beside the seal, enforce RED IS NEVER EMPTY on that file, then rename it over the seal. A rename on one filesystem is atomic, so the in-flight seal stands until the whole red seal replaces it, and no reader ever sees an empty one. The green path, which empties an in-flight seal in one write, already moves from one standing state to another. An arm should read the seal from a second process across a red run's close, and see it read red or in flight, never green.
